summary:
Senate Bill 150, enacted on 29 March 2023 after the General Assembly overrode Governor Andy Beshear's veto, carries Kentucky's restriction on which bathrooms transgender students may use in public schools alongside its ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender minors. It is the single 2023 statute containing the K-12 facility restriction, and the Movement Advancement Project's equality map lists it among state-level bans on transgender people using public facilities according to gender identity. The facility provision is written for public school students; the sources reviewed identify no statewide rule governing adult use of bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Responsibility for carrying out the school restriction sits with local districts. The Kentucky Department of Education issued guidance in April 2023 for districts implementing the state's 2023 rules, advising them to remove sex education from the fifth-grade curriculum and to proceed cautiously with the bathroom provisions.

The care ban took effect on 14 July 2023, when U.S. District Judge David Hale lifted the injunction he had issued the previous month, barring transgender minors from puberty blockers and hormone therapy. Seven transgender children and their parents had sued to block the law, and the ACLU of Kentucky described the ruling as a temporary setback. On 28 September 2023 a federal appeals panel allowed the ban to remain in force while challenges proceed. Minors already receiving care were given no phase-out.

Birth certificates can be amended only for post-operative applicants: a doctor's letter stating that gender-affirming surgery has been performed goes directly to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort. A court order was previously required for a Kentucky-born person.

School sport is closed to transgender girls under Senate Bill 83, which passed the General Assembly in March 2022, was vetoed by Governor Beshear in April 2022 on constitutionality and vagueness grounds, and was enacted over that veto the same month with immediate effect. House Bill 470, carrying the minors' care ban among other provisions, advanced on 2 March 2023 and passed on 17 March 2023, was vetoed, and was overridden on 29 March 2023 by simple majority votes; police arrested 19 capitol protesters for criminal trespassing that day.

Employment protection derives from federal appellate and executive sources rather than from statute. On 7 March 2018 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, which covers Kentucky, held in EEOC v. R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars firing an employee for being transgender or for transitioning, because it penalises failure to conform to birth-assigned sex stereotypes, and that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act does not permit a private employer to dismiss a transgender worker on religious grounds. The case arose from funeral director Aimee Stephens, dismissed in 2013 after disclosing her planned transition. A June 2008 executive order barred hiring or firing state employees on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, restoring protections first issued in 2003 and removed in 2006. Nineteen cities maintain Fairness Ordinances covering gender identity in employment, housing and public accommodations.

Kentucky's hate-crime statutes cover sexual orientation and expressly exclude gender identity, so bias-motivated violence against a transgender person falls outside the state's hate-crime enhancement. The sexual-orientation provision was used in the April 2011 beating of Kevin Pennington at Kingdom Come State Park near Cumberland, which produced arrests on 15 March 2012 by Kentucky State Police working with the FBI and guilty pleas from two defendants after advocacy by the Kentucky Equality Federation.

Conversion therapy on minors has been illegal statewide since Governor Beshear's executive order of 18 September 2024, following city bans in Covington (March 2020, 5-0), Louisville (September 2020, 24-1) and Lexington (May 2021, unanimous).

Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since the Kentucky Supreme Court struck down KRS 510.100 in Kentucky v. Wasson in 1992 on state constitutional grounds, a result reinforced by Lawrence v. Texas in 2003. The unenforceable statute remains on the books; it formerly punished specified sexual acts as a misdemeanour carrying up to 12 months in jail and a $500 fine, with solicitation punishable by up to 90 days and $250.

Religious-exemption and service-access rules cut against those protections. The 2013 Religious Freedom Act requires the state to show clear and convincing evidence before burdening a sincerely held religious belief; Governor Beshear vetoed it over vagueness and the risk of overriding local non-discrimination ordinances, and the General Assembly overrode him 79-15 in the House and 32-6 in the Senate. Senate Bill 17, signed by Governor Matt Bevin in March 2017, allows religious student organisations use of school facilities and control of their internal affairs. In August 2020 a district court held that a Christian photographer, as a public business, could not be compelled to photograph same-sex weddings because the photographs are art and speech protected against compulsion.
tangentialFactors:
Kentucky's protections are a patchwork rather than a floor. Employment protection rests on a federal appellate ruling and an executive order limited to state employees, while the hate-crime statute omits gender identity and the 2013 Religious Freedom Act gives religious claims a statutory route around local ordinances.

Coverage of the Fairness Ordinances is municipal, not statewide. Outside the 19 listed cities there is no local public-accommodations protection on gender identity, and the statewide non-discrimination guarantee for public employment does not reach private employers.

The Sixth Circuit's 2018 holding governs Kentucky along with the other states in that circuit, so the workplace position in Kentucky turns on federal appellate and Supreme Court litigation rather than on action by the General Assembly.
localsOnly:
Amending a Kentucky birth certificate requires a doctor's letter confirming gender-affirming surgery, sent to the Department of Vital Statistics in Frankfort; a court order is no longer the route for a Kentucky-born person.

Minors cannot obtain puberty blockers or hormone therapy in Kentucky, with no phase-out for those already in treatment, and the ban has stayed in force through appellate review since September 2023.

State employees are protected against hiring or firing discrimination on gender identity by executive order dating to 2008. Private-sector employees in the 19 Fairness Ordinance cities have local recourse in employment, housing and public accommodations; elsewhere they rely on the Sixth Circuit's Title VII holding.

Bias crimes against transgender residents are not covered by the state hate-crime statute, which lists sexual orientation but not gender identity.

Conversion therapy on minors is barred statewide by executive order since September 2024.

Transgender students in public schools are restricted to facilities matching their birth-assigned sex under the 2023 statute, with compliance left to district-level decisions guided by the April 2023 education department advice.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the appellate status of the 2023 care ban has changed since September 2023 is not established by the sources reviewed.

No source in the inventory quantifies enforcement of the school facility provision, records exclusionary or disciplinary incidents under it, or reports trans-specific violence statistics for Kentucky.

The scope of Title VII protection as applied in Kentucky following later federal litigation is unresolved in these sources.

Whether the surgery requirement for birth-certificate amendment has been litigated or administratively revised is not sourced.

No source addresses how the 2013 Religious Freedom Act has been applied to transgender-specific service refusals in Kentucky.
